core: transparent terms and bounded legal/fairness context

claims.claim: Pricing policy can be organized around objectives such as customer value, cost, sales orientation, market share, target return, competition, and customer considerations; an organization can have more than one objective.
A basic single-offering break-even calculation in units is fixed costs divided by unit price minus variable cost per unit.

In a basic cost-volume-profit model, fixed costs are fixed in total and variable costs are fixed per unit only over a relevant range; simple analysis relies on stated assumptions such as constant price and, for multiple products, stable sales mix.

Federal Trade Commission guidance says advertising claims must be truthful, nondeceptive, fair, and evidence-based; its small-business guide identifies price representations as material claims and applies truthfulness standards to price comparisons and sale prices.

Federal Robinson-Patman price-discrimination analysis applies under specific conditions and involves complex legal tests and defenses, so it cannot determine the legality of a real practice from a simplified classroom description.
A break-even result is conditional on its model inputs and does not by itself forecast demand, establish capacity, include every relevant cost, or recommend a price.

A price test can be confounded by changes in audience, channel, timing, message, or offer, so findings should be limited to the tested conditions rather than presented as universal willingness-to-pay facts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether different prices are inherently unfair or unlawful
positions: A classroom intuition may equate any different price with unfairness.
FTC guidance explains that Robinson-Patman analysis is conditional, includes legal tests and defenses, and does not make every price difference a violation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not provide a compliance rule. It distinguishes transparent, explainable terms as an educational fairness principle from formal legal analysis, which is jurisdiction- and fact-dependent.
